claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is fully homogenized as a high-temperature BCC phase after solution treatment above approximately 1100°C.
The phases formed during cooling and thermal exposure are governed by rate-dependent atomic ordering and elemental partitioning.
Al partitioning and its coupled diffusion with other alloying elements drive the proposed phase evolution.
Slow cooling and subsequent thermal holds permit Al segregation.
Al segregation induces short-range order, including possible B2-like ordering or related intermetallic precipitation.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps a homogeneous BCC state by arresting diffusion.
Differential atomic mobility during cooling allows Al, potentially together with other elements, to segregate into locally ordered domains.
Enhanced atomic mobility during slow cooling nucleates multiple ordered phases.
A slow-cooled sample subsequently held at 600°C for 10 hours will contain ordered precipitates or secondary phases relative to a quenched baseline.
The quenched baseline will remain a single, chemically homogeneous BCC phase.
The predicted secondary phases or ordering will produce additional diffraction reflections, ordered domains, or local compositional modulations detectable by XRD, TEM, or atom-probe tomography.
The proposed mechanism applies when cooling or thermal exposure provides sufficient atomic mobility for ordering and segregation.
The proposed mechanism should not produce phase evolution under extreme quenching or other conditions that restrict diffusion.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloys with compositions significantly different from Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The exact composition and crystal structure of the proposed ordered phases are uncertain.
The roles of Ni, Co, and Fe in the Al-associated ordering pathway are uncertain because competing diffusion kinetics and ordering pathways may exist.
